hints: Look at Fig. 4.1 - the signal travels out along the inner copper core, so think about what a complete circuit needs for the current to come back.
Think about why the braid completely surrounds the core - what outside influences on a TV signal would a surrounding metal layer block?
walkthrough:
**Why Two Conductors Are Needed**
Think of the cable as part of a complete circuit. The inner copper core carries the signal from the aerial to the receiver, but current must have a return path. The copper braid is that second conductor, coaxial with the core and separated from it by the insulator.

**Why The Braid Surrounds The Core**
A TV signal is very small and easily spoiled by external electromagnetic noise and by crosstalk from nearby cables. Because the braid is made of conducting copper and completely encloses the core, it acts as an electrostatic shield, picking up or reflecting unwanted waves before they reach the core.
Final answer: 1. Acts as the return conductor for the signal. 2. Provides shielding of the inner core from external noise / interference / crosstalk.

hints: Compare the construction of an open wire pair with a coaxial cable - which one has a metal shield around the signal wire?
A TV signal needs a very high frequency range to carry picture and sound - think about which type of cable can support a large bandwidth with low loss.
walkthrough:
**No Shielding Means Noise**
A wire pair is just two unshielded wires side by side. Unlike the coaxial braid, there is nothing to screen the signal. It easily picks up external electromagnetic interference and crosstalk from other wire pairs, which degrades the analogue TV picture and sound.

**Poor High-Frequency Performance**
A TV signal requires a large bandwidth at high frequencies. A wire pair has a much smaller bandwidth than coaxial cable and suffers large attenuation, so the signal power falls rapidly and the high-frequency detail is lost.
Final answer: Any two from: small bandwidth, susceptible to noise / interference / crosstalk, large attenuation / energy loss, reflections due to poor impedance matching.

hints: Start with the total loss in dB - check the units carefully, attenuation is given per km but the length is only 14 m.
Recall how attenuation in dB is linked to input and output powers using a base-10 logarithm.
Rearrange the log equation to find the power ratio $P_{OUT}/P_{IN}$ - remember to handle the minus sign for a loss.
Be careful to distinguish the fraction that remains from the fraction that is lost - loss means input minus output divided by input.
walkthrough:
**Find The Total Attenuation In dB**
Attenuation adds up along the cable. Convert length to km: $$14\text{ m} = 0.014\text{ km}$$ Then: $$\text{attenuation} = 190 \times 0.014 = 2.66\text{ dB}$$ This is the total loss in signal level from aerial to receiver.

**Use The Decibel Law For Power**
For power, attenuation in dB is defined by: $$\text{attenuation (dB)} = 10\lg\left(\frac{P_{IN}}{P_{OUT}}\right) = -10\lg\left(\frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}}\right)$$ So: $$2.66 = 10\lg\left(\frac{P_{IN}}{P_{OUT}}\right)$$

**Calculate The Power Ratio**
Divide by 10 and take antilog: $$\lg\left(\frac{P_{IN}}{P_{OUT}}\right) = 0.266$$ $$\frac{P_{IN}}{P_{OUT}} = 10^{0.266} \approx 1.85$$ Invert to get the fraction transmitted: $$\frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}} = \frac{1}{1.85} \approx 0.54$$ Only about half the power arrives.

**Convert To Fractional Loss**
Fractional loss is what is missing, not what remains: $$\text{fractional loss} = \frac{P_{IN} - P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}} = 1 - \frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}}$$ $$= 1 - 0.54 = 0.46$$ About 46% of the signal power is lost in the 14 m cable.
Final answer: Total attenuation $= 2.66\text{ dB}$, $P_{OUT}/P_{IN} = 0.54$, fractional loss $= 1 - 0.54 = 0.46$.
